name: L-Cysteine

lead: L-cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that the body can make from methionine and that is also supplied by protein-rich foods. It is sold as a supplement and used in food processing, and its acetylated form N-acetylcysteine is a well-known medicine.
In skin-tone discussions it is mentioned as a glutathione precursor and because cysteine participates in melanin pathways. Evidence that it lightens skin is limited and mostly indirect.

paras: Cysteine is the rate-limiting amino acid for glutathione synthesis. Its availability is also thought to steer melanocytes toward pheomelanin, the lighter pigment, rather than eumelanin. Whether supplemental doses meaningfully change visible pigmentation in people is unproven.

Typical dietary and low-dose supplemental intake is generally tolerated, with possible gastrointestinal upset. High doses can cause nausea and other effects, and people with cystinuria or on certain medications are advised to seek medical advice before use. Products marketed for lightening are not approved for that use.

lead: Cysteine is a semiessential proteinogenic amino acid whose side chain carries a thiol (sulfhydryl) group. The L-form is a building block of proteins in all organisms; the thiol lets cysteine residues form disulfide bonds that stabilize protein structure, as in keratin, and bind metal ions [1]. Humans can usually make it from methionine through the transsulfuration pathway, and it is also supplied by foods such as poultry, eggs, beef and whole grains [1].

In appearance-related discussion, L-cysteine comes up mainly as a precursor of glutathione, the cell's principal thiol antioxidant, and because cysteine availability is proposed to influence which melanin type is made in skin. It is sold as a supplement, appears in hair supplements, and has industrial uses in food processing and in permanent-wave hair treatments [1]. Its acetylated derivative, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), is a long-established medicine used as a mucolytic and as an antidote to paracetamol poisoning [2].

No published human trial in the reference material tests supplemental L-cysteine itself for skin lightening or other cosmetic outcomes. Evidence for a pigment effect is indirect, drawn from biochemistry and from studies of related compounds.

paras: Cysteine has the formula HS-CH2-CH(NH2)-COOH. Its thiol is readily oxidized, and two cysteines linked by a disulfide bond form cystine [1]. The name derives from the Greek word for bladder, because it was first found in urinary stones [1].

In animals, synthesis starts from serine, with sulfur supplied by methionine via homocysteine; cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase complete the pathway [1]. Cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency lowers levels of cysteine, glutathione, taurine and hydrogen sulfide in cells [3].

Cysteine is the sulfur-containing precursor for glutathione. The Wikipedia article notes that orally supplied glutathione has negligible systemic availability, so the body must synthesize it from cysteine, glycine and glutamate, and that dietary cysteine and glycine can improve synthesis [1]. Cysteine also supplies sulfide for iron-sulfur clusters and is the source of endogenous hydrogen sulfide, a signalling molecule studied in the nervous and cardiovascular systems [1][4].

Skin-tone discussions mention cysteine because the pigment pathway is thought to produce lighter pheomelanin when cysteine is available, and because it feeds glutathione production. These are proposed mechanisms rather than demonstrated effects of oral cysteine in human skin.

In hair care, cysteine is used in permanent-wave products, chiefly in Asia, where it breaks disulfide bonds in keratin [1]. Some forum posters recommend cysteine-containing supplements for hair growth [5].

L-Cysteine is a processing aid in baking and a precursor for savoury flavors made through Maillard reactions [1]. It is mostly produced by hydrolysis of animal material such as poultry feathers or hog hair, with synthetic and fermentation routes available for kosher, halal or vegetarian use [1].

NAC is used as a mucolytic and for acetaminophen poisoning, where it restores depleted liver glutathione, and has been studied for respiratory disease and neuropsychiatric conditions [2][6]. A US drug label for an oral L-cysteine homeopathic product lists traditional symptom-relief statements and notes that homeopathic statements are not FDA-evaluated [7].

No studies found on L-cysteine as a skin-lightening or other appearance agent. Human research on cysteine and NAC concerns medical conditions, including a randomized trial of NAC in Parkinson's disease [8], an NAC trial in sudden deafness [9], a phase 3 study of L-cysteine in erythropoietic protoporphyria [10], and small phase 1 and 2 registrations of L-cysteine in healthy lactating women, peritoneal dialysis patients, and atrophic gastritis [11][12][13]. Reviews describe antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity of NAC in respiratory disease [6].

Cysteine from food is part of normal protein intake. Supplement and label information sources advise asking a healthcare professional before use during pregnancy or breastfeeding [7]. A case report describes a fixed drug eruption caused by S-carboxymethyl-L-cysteine, a related mucolytic [14]. Detailed adverse-event rates for supplemental L-cysteine are not covered by the studies cited here.

On T Nation, L-cysteine is mentioned in several contexts: as a supplement some members used for low SHBG while on anabolic steroids [15][16], as part of a stack for irritability and sleep [17], in hair-growth advice [5], and as a glutathione and liver-support precursor via NAC [18]. A 2021 thread discussed a regulatory change affecting NAC supplements in the US [19].

lore.intro: On forums, L-cysteine appears as a supplement-stack ingredient and as a glutathione precursor, usually mentioned in passing rather than as a primary appearance tool [15][17][18].
